variants.name: JPA/Hibernate version token
variants.implementation_notes: Scala's mainstream persistence stacks sit on Hibernate/JPA, so the token mechanism is available unchanged: annotate one mutable field (@Version var version: Long = 0) and the provider adds the version predicate to every generated UPDATE/DELETE, reporting a stale write as OptimisticLockException (or the legacy StaleObjectStateException); Hibernate additionally offers @OptimisticLocking(DIRTY|ALL) for schemas without a version column. The classic structure disappears behind the mapping, which is why the Scala-specific work is keeping the version in a mutable field the provider can update.
pitfalls: An immutable case class forces a copy instead of a managed update, so the provider has no mutable version field to increment and detection disappears.
The exception marks the session for rollback: any retry must open a new session/transaction.
Bulk JPQL/HQL and native SQL updates skip the token, exactly as in Java - the escape hatches are where stale writes get through.

variants.name: Concurrent collection conditional update
variants.implementation_notes: Scala's concurrent collections provide the in-process form: scala.collection.concurrent.Map guarantees that all changes are atomic, with TrieMap as the lock-free hash-trie implementation offering O(1) lock-free snapshots. A conditional update on such a map - replacing a value only if it still holds the expected version - is a compare-and-set over a versioned slot and can serve as the token registry for a process-local edit session; it replaces the persisted token only while the session never leaves the process.
pitfalls: Atomicity covers one key, not a cluster: validating several records needs an immutable snapshot behind a single atomic reference or an STM transaction.
getOrElse + replace is only safe because replace re-checks the old value - a get followed by put reintroduces the lost update.
The map holds the token, not the data: without a single-writer discipline for the record itself the CAS proves nothing about the payload.
